constitutive_assumptions: Strain occurs only at the thin-membrane face of the elastomer actuator chambers.
The entire membrane face is in contact with the opposing face during actuation (Ac = Af).
The effect of joint bending angle on the moment arm is negligible.
The strain-limiting layer is flexible but inextensible.
Chamber pressure is uniform throughout an individual actuator.
control_variables: Outer actuator dimensions along finger length (width 2 cm and length 6 cm for two-finger version; width 3.6 cm and length 8 cm for three-finger version)
Elastomer wall thicknesses (thin membrane wall thickness 0.9 mm; other walls >= 2.5 mm)
Internal chamber spacing (2 mm wide chambers with 0.56 mm gaps formed by polycarbonate strips)
Silicone materials (DragonSkin-20 for actuator chambers and structural layers; MoldStar-30 for directional adhesive wedges)
Spin-coating speeds and times (800 rpm for 1 minute for structural layers; 400 rpm for 2 minutes for bonding)
Cure temperature and duration for adhesive daughter molds (20 minutes at 50 °C for partial cure)
Target object material for grasp pullout tests (polycarbonate cylinders)
dependent_variables: Real contact area (measured via Frustrated Total Internal Reflection)
Grasp pullout force / grip strength / lift force

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Integrating directional gecko-inspired adhesives onto fluidic elastomer actuators decouples grasp strength from high normal force and high internal fluid pressure by leveraging adhesion-controlled friction.

Fluidic elastomer actuators can be modeled as a series of discrete joints where joint torque depends on internal pressure, membrane area, and neutral axis distance, enabling actuators to follow a modified Hirose torque distribution that maintains surface contact area under pressurization.

Using Frustrated Total Internal Reflection (FTIR), an actuator designed with a Hirose torque distribution maintained high contact area across increasing pressures, whereas an actuator with a uniform torque profile lost contact as distal joints overpowered proximal joints.

In cylinder pullout tests at 27 kPa, the gecko elastomer actuator gripper produced 35.7 N higher grasp force on a 57 mm cylinder (348% increase) and 8.58 N higher force on a 203 mm cylinder (2095% increase) compared to an identical non-adhesive elastomer gripper.

On dusty, rocky, or irregular objects where adhesive performance is diminished, the gecko elastomer actuator gripper maintains baseline force-closure functionality with no measured loss in performance relative to conventional elastomer grippers.

A three-finger gecko elastomer gripper mounted on a KUKA LBR iiwa robot arm supported and manipulated an 11.3 kg (111 N / 25 lbf) payload at 40 kPa internal pressure across more than 25 trials without visible damage or performance loss.

Directional gecko adhesives require shear loading to engage; on curved surfaces shear is induced passively by object geometry, whereas flat surfaces lack passive shear and require high bending stiffness or actuation-independent stiffening mechanisms.

experimental_setup: Single-joint torque bench: 3D-printed brackets holding an elastomer joint at fixed angles (0 deg, 10 deg, 20 deg) with a fixed moment arm while internal pressure is varied and output force is recorded with a Mark-10 M5-10 force gauge.

Contact area measurement apparatus: cylindrical Frustrated Total Internal Reflection (FTIR) sensor illuminated by white LEDs around the cylinder rim and recorded by an axial wide-angle camera with dark frame subtraction calibration.

Cylindrical object pullout test: two-finger gripper (2 cm x 6 cm actuators) gripping polycarbonate cylinders of varying diameters (57 mm to 203 mm) at varying pressures (e.g., 27 kPa and pressure sweeps) while measuring pullout force with a Mark-10 force gauge.

Robotic manipulation and high-load testbed: three-finger gripper (actuators 3.6 cm x 8 cm with nylon/carbon-fiber composite brackets) mounted on a teleoperated KUKA LBR iiwa robotic arm, picking, translating, and releasing an 11.3 kg mass at 40 kPa chamber pressure across over 25 trials.
future_work: Applying surface-conformation and torque-profile modeling methods broadly to other fluidic elastomer actuators.
Integrating actuation-independent stiffening mechanisms (such as jamming components or phase-transition elements) to enable effective adhesive grasping on flat surfaces.
Extending gecko elastomer actuators into industrial automation and other high-load manipulation applications.
independent_variables: Surface presence of gecko-inspired adhesive (gecko vs. non-gecko elastomer actuator)
Designed joint torque profile (Hirose distribution vs. uniform torque distribution)
Gripper finger count and actuator surface area (two-finger 2 cm x 6 cm vs. three-finger 3.6 cm x 8 cm)
limitations_inferred: Testing was restricted to smooth polycarbonate cylinders and a small number of rigid household items, leaving performance on compliant, rough, or delicate textured surfaces uncharacterized.
Long-term interfacial fatigue and delamination risks between the DragonSkin and MoldStar silicone layers under repeated shear loading were not evaluated beyond 25 manipulation cycles.
Disengagement dynamics, release speed, and passive release reliability under transient or perturbing shear loads were not systematically measured.
Manual manufacturing steps involving polycarbonate shims and spin-coating may result in fabrication variability between individual actuator fingers.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The joint torque model assumes strain is localized to the thin membrane, full membrane contact occurs, and joint angle effects on moment arm are negligible, causing model inaccuracies including overprediction at low pressures/higher joint angles and underprediction at high pressures due to membrane bulging.
Adhesion is temporarily degraded by dust, dirt, or porous surfaces (though cleanable using a tacky surface).
Because elastomer actuators possess low inherent bending stiffness, adhesive performance on flat surfaces is poor without active shear preloads or actuation-independent stiffening mechanisms.
Directional wedge adhesives require a shear load to engage, precluding normal-only engagement without active or geometric shear generation.
The torque model serves primarily as a design tool for geometry rather than for real-time state estimation and control.
Manufacturing chambers with 0.9 mm membrane walls and 2 mm chamber widths approached the practical limits of the casting process.
main_results: The analytical joint torque model closely matched measured single-joint torque at 0 deg, with discrepancies at non-zero angles and higher pressures explained by non-linear membrane bulging and initial contact gaps.

FTIR imaging verified that an actuator fabricated with a Hirose-derived torque profile maintained high contact area throughout pressurization, whereas a uniform torque profile actuator lifted away from the surface.

Gecko elastomer actuators demonstrated substantial increases in pullout force over non-adhesive actuators across all tested cylinder diameters at 27 kPa, including a 348% increase (35.7 N higher) on a 57 mm cylinder and a 2095% increase (8.58 N higher) on a 203 mm cylinder.
On large cylinders where wrap grasps are impossible, the gecko gripper provided an additional 6.5 N of grip force across all tested pressures due to adhesion-controlled friction.
A high-load three-finger gecko gripper supported an 11.3 kg (111 N / 25 lbf) payload at an internal pressure of only 40 kPa on a KUKA LBR iiwa robotic arm.

On dusty and rocky surfaces where adhesives do not engage, the gripper preserved the baseline force-closure grasping performance of standard fluidic elastomer grippers without measurable performance loss.
A two-finger actuator pair achieved a 270 deg bend in 400 ms at 50 kPa using 31.4 mJ of energy, weighing 48.7 g with $7.25 in raw material costs.
modeling_methods: Discrete joint approximation of fluidic elastomer actuators with associated joint torques.

Hirose torque distribution criterion limiting actuator joint torque along finger length to prevent outer joints from overpowering inner joints and maintain surface contact: tau(s) = tau0 * (1 - s/L)^2.
Analytical joint torque formulation relating internal pressure, contact face area, and centroid distance: tau_joint = P * Af * d.
Semicircular chamber geometric model determining internal chamber radius distribution along the finger length: r(s) = r0 * (1 - s/L)^(2/3).
performance_metrics: Maximum payload / grasp lift force (over 50 N for two-finger gripper; 111 N / 25 lbf for three-finger gripper)
Grasp pullout force improvement over non-adhesive actuators (348% increase on 57 mm cylinder; 2095% increase on 203 mm cylinder)
Operating internal fluid pressure (17 kPa for 270 deg free bending; 27 kPa for cylinder tests; 40 kPa for 111 N payload lift)
Actuation speed / bending duration (under 0.4 s / 400 ms for 270 deg bend)
Actuation energy input (15.7 mJ for a single finger; 31.4 mJ for two fingers to bend 270 deg)
Contact area retention under varying pressure (evaluated qualitatively and quantitatively via FTIR brightness)
Gripper mass (48.7 g for two-finger unit)
Raw material fabrication cost ($7.25 per unit)
Cycle repeatability (over 25 pick-and-place trials without visible plastic deformation or performance loss)
possible_gap_implications: Integrating active or actuation-independent stiffening mechanisms (such as granular or layer jamming) could allow gecko elastomer grippers to effectively preload and adhere to flat surfaces without sacrificing compliance.

Formulating elastomeric continuum or nonlinear finite element models that account for membrane bulging and non-zero joint angles could refine joint torque predictions for advanced closed-loop control.
Developing automated or monolithic manufacturing approaches could reduce fabrication variance and facilitate micro-chamber scaling beyond manual casting limits.
paper.research_objective: To investigate the integration of fluidic elastomer actuators with directional gecko-inspired adhesives to enable high-strength grasping at low operating pressures, expand grasping capabilities to objects too large to enclose via adhesion-controlled friction, and maintain surface contact area through analytical joint-torque design while preserving standard soft gripper compliance and force-closure on non-adhesive surfaces.
paper.research_problem: Fluidic elastomer actuators face fundamental trade-offs in grasping large objects and achieving high-strength grasps because their load capacity relies on friction bounded by actuator bending stiffness and normal force; conventional solutions increase internal pressure, which causes high energy consumption, transmission delays, risk of rupture, reduced surface conformation, and limited control authority.
stiffness_mechanism: fluid pressure stiffening (pressurization of internal elastomer chambers)
strain-limiting layer (flexible but inextensible embedded polyester mesh)
rigid mounting brackets and anchors (nylon/carbon-fiber composite brackets and 3-D printed anchors)
paper.title: A Soft Robotic Gripper With Gecko-Inspired Adhesive
